notes:
Chapter overview

Women’s anti-colonial participation moved from Sivaganga’s armed restoration to suffrage, Gandhian mass action, imprisonment, cultural mobilisation, Quit India and the Rani of Jhansi Regiment.

Early leadershipPolitical citizenshipMass movementsCultural mobilisationINA & diaspora
Scope, Phases and Sources

Women’s participation ranged from eighteenth-century armed leadership to suffrage campaigns, Gandhian mass action, imprisonment, cultural mobilisation and overseas INA service.

Scope

Women participated in Tamil Nadu’s anti-colonial struggle in several different capacities:

  • Rulers and military commanders
  • Satyagrahis
  • Political organisers
  • Congress volunteers
  • Journalists and editors
  • Speakers and writers
  • Singers and theatre artists
  • Khadi workers
  • Foreign-cloth and liquor-shop picketers
  • Prisoners
  • Underground activists
  • Doctors and nurses
  • Indian National Army personnel

Their participation extended from the Sivaganga resistance of the eighteenth century to the INA campaign during the Second World War.

Major Phases
Early Armed Resistance

Women such as Velu Nachiyar and Kuyili were associated with armed resistance against Company expansion.

Political Awakening

Women entered public life through:

  • Women’s organisations
  • Suffrage campaigns
  • Home Rule meetings
  • Political conferences
  • Journalism
  • Public speaking
Gandhian Mass Movements

Women participated in:

  • Non-Cooperation
  • Khadi promotion
  • Foreign-cloth boycott
  • Liquor-shop picketing
  • Salt Satyagraha
  • Civil Disobedience
  • Individual Satyagraha
  • Quit India
Overseas Armed Nationalism

Tamil women in Malaya, Singapore and Burma joined or supported:

  • Indian Independence League
  • Indian National Army
  • Rani of Jhansi Regiment
Madras Presidency Context

The Madras Presidency included territories outside present-day Tamil Nadu. Women described in records as belonging to “Madras” may have come from areas now situated in:

  • Tamil Nadu
  • Kerala
  • Andhra Pradesh
  • Karnataka

The chapter therefore prioritises women directly connected with Tamil Nadu or with Tamil communities overseas.

Sources

Important sources include:

  • Colonial police reports
  • Prison registers
  • Trial records
  • Congress proceedings
  • Women’s organisation records
  • Newspapers and journals
  • Autobiographies
  • Family accounts
  • Oral traditions
  • INA memoirs
  • Memorial publications

Women’s contributions are often under-recorded because official reports concentrated on prominent leaders and treated activities such as cooking, sheltering activists, fundraising and carrying messages as secondary.

Velu Nachiyar and Kuyili in Early Armed Resistance

Velu Nachiyar led the restoration of Sivaganga, while Kuyili is remembered as a commander associated with the attack on an enemy ammunition store; the topic emphasises women’s leadership rather than repeating Chapter 18’s full military chronology.

Velu Nachiyar

Velu Nachiyar was the queen of Sivaganga.

Important facts:

  • She was born in 1730 into the Ramanathapuram royal family.
  • She was trained in horse riding, archery and weapon use.
  • She married Muthu Vaduganatha Thevar, ruler of Sivaganga.
  • Company and Nawab forces attacked Kalaiyar Kovil in 1772.
  • Muthu Vaduganatha Thevar was killed.
  • Velu Nachiyar escaped with her daughter Vellachi.
  • She took refuge under Gopala Nayak at Virupachi.
  • She secured assistance from Hyder Ali.
  • The Marudhu Brothers assisted her military reorganisation.
  • She recovered Sivaganga and returned to power in 1780.

Velu Nachiyar represented women’s political and military leadership in an age when resistance was organised through kingdoms, Palayams and armed alliances.

Intelligence and Military Organisation

Velu Nachiyar:

  • Recruited and reorganised troops
  • Sent agents to gather intelligence
  • Identified enemy military positions
  • Maintained alliances with neighbouring chiefs
  • Used Mysore assistance against Company forces

Her resistance was directed at restoring Sivaganga’s sovereignty rather than participating in the later Congress-led national movement.

Kuyili

Kuyili is remembered as:

  • A trusted associate of Velu Nachiyar
  • Commander of a women’s military unit
  • A participant in the attack on the enemy arsenal

The Tamil Nadu textbook states that Kuyili entered the British ammunition store after setting herself on fire and destroyed the ammunition.

This account is strongly preserved in Tamil commemorative tradition. The lack of extensive contemporary documentation should be acknowledged.

Udaiyaal

Tamil tradition also remembers Udaiyaal, a shepherd girl who was killed after refusing to reveal information about Velu Nachiyar’s movements.

Chapter Boundary

This topic focuses on the significance of women’s leadership.

Detailed treatment of:

  • Kalaiyar Kovil
  • Virupachi
  • Hyder Ali’s assistance
  • Recovery of Sivaganga
  • Military chronology

belongs to Chapter 18.

Women’s Political Awakening, Organisations and Suffrage

Women’s organisations transformed education and social reform into political citizenship by demanding franchise, legal equality and entry into legislatures.

Women’s entry into organised politics was assisted by education, reform associations, printing, Home Rule and the campaign for voting rights.

Women’s India Association

The Women’s India Association was established at Adyar, Madras, in 1917.

The Tamil Nadu textbook identifies its principal founders as:

  • Annie Besant
  • Dorothy Jinarajadasa
  • Margaret Cousins

Ammu Swaminathan, Muthulakshmi Reddy and other women were closely connected with its establishment and expansion.

Major Objectives

The association addressed:

  • Women’s education
  • Voting rights
  • Marriage laws
  • Child marriage
  • Women’s health
  • Childcare
  • Women’s public participation
  • Property and legal rights
  • Devadasi dedication

It circulated:

  • Pamphlets
  • Bulletins
  • Articles in multiple languages
Women’s Franchise

Women’s organisations argued that political freedom could not be complete while women were denied voting rights.

Their campaigns demanded:

  • Women’s inclusion in the electorate
  • Equal civic status
  • Entry into legislatures
  • Recognition of women as political citizens
All India Women’s Conference

The All India Women’s Conference emerged in 1927 with an initial emphasis on women’s education.

It later addressed:

  • Legal reform
  • Social reform
  • Political representation
  • Women’s rights
Importance to the Freedom Struggle

Women’s organisations:

  • Trained women in public speaking
  • Created province-wide networks
  • Organised conferences
  • Introduced women to constitutional politics
  • Connected national independence with women’s equality

Detailed legal and social-reform campaigns belong mainly to Chapters 20 and 21.

Thillaiyadi Valliammai and South African Satyagraha

Thillaiyadi Valliammai connected Tamil migrant history with Gandhi’s South African Satyagraha and died after imprisonment at the age of sixteen.

Identity

Valliamma Munuswami Mudaliar is popularly known as:

  • Thillaiyadi Valliammai

She was born in Johannesburg on 22 February 1898 to a Tamil migrant family with roots in Thillaiyadi.

The place-name association comes from her family’s Tamil origin; Valliammai herself grew up in South Africa.

Background of the Agitation

Indian communities in South Africa faced:

  • Racial discrimination
  • Pass restrictions
  • Movement controls
  • Discriminatory taxation
  • Non-recognition of Indian marriages

A 1913 court judgement threatened the legal recognition of Hindu, Muslim and other non-Christian marriages.

Indian women entered Gandhi’s Satyagraha in protest.

Valliammai’s Participation
  • Valliammai joined the campaign with her mother.
  • She travelled with women campaigners across mining and settlement areas.
  • They encouraged Indian workers to join the resistance.
  • The women crossed provincial boundaries without official permission.
  • Valliammai was arrested.
  • She was sentenced to three months of hard labour at Pietermaritzburg prison.
Imprisonment and Death
  • Valliammai became seriously ill in prison.
  • She refused to abandon the struggle in return for an early release.
  • She was released in February 1914.
  • She died on 22 February 1914, her sixteenth birthday.

Gandhi later remembered her courage in his account of the South African Satyagraha.

Importance

Thillaiyadi Valliammai demonstrates that Tamil women’s anti-colonial participation extended beyond India.

She is associated with:

  • Tamil migrant history
  • South African Satyagraha
  • Women’s civil resistance
  • Indian opposition to racial discrimination

Do not state that she was born in the village of Thillaiyadi; stronger historical accounts place her birth in Johannesburg.

Women in Swadeshi, Home Rule and Non-Cooperation

Swadeshi, Home Rule and Non-Cooperation expanded women’s political role through household boycott, khadi, public meetings, fundraising, picketing and constructive work.

Swadeshi Participation

The Swadeshi Movement encouraged women to convert household practices into political action.

Women participated by:

  • Rejecting foreign cloth
  • Wearing indigenous textiles
  • Promoting hand-spun cloth
  • Attending nationalist meetings
  • Raising funds
  • Teaching children nationalist songs
  • Supporting Swadeshi enterprises

Women’s control over household purchases made the foreign-goods boycott particularly significant.

Annie Besant and Home Rule

Annie Besant used Madras as an important centre of the Home Rule Movement.

Her methods included:

  • Public speeches
  • Newspapers
  • Home Rule classes
  • Political branches
  • Student mobilisation
  • Women’s organisation

Important publications:

  • New India
  • Commonweal

Her internment in 1917 generated protests and increased support for Home Rule.

Women in Non-Cooperation

During the Non-Cooperation Movement, women joined:

  • Khadi work
  • Foreign-cloth boycott
  • Liquor-shop picketing
  • Fundraising
  • Public processions
  • National education
  • Congress volunteer work
Constructive Work

Women’s political contribution was not limited to street demonstrations.

They also:

  • Spun yarn
  • Distributed khadi
  • Organised women’s meetings
  • Collected jewellery and donations
  • Taught literacy
  • Supported prisoners’ families
  • Provided food and shelter to volunteers
Historical Importance

Swadeshi and Gandhian constructive work made political participation possible within both public and domestic spaces.

Women who had not previously entered formal politics could contribute through everyday economic choices and community organisation.

Rukmini Lakshmipathi and the Salt Satyagraha

Rukmini Lakshmipathi linked suffrage activism, Congress politics, direct salt-law violation and later legislative responsibility.

Early Public Life

Rukmini Lakshmipathi was born in Madras in 1892.

Important associations:

  • Women’s Christian College
  • Bharat Stree Mahamandal
  • Indian National Congress
  • Women’s political representation
  • Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha

She joined the Congress in 1923.

She also represented Indian women at an international women’s suffrage conference in Paris in 1926.

Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha

In 1930:

  • Rajaji led the Salt March from Tiruchirappalli to Vedaranyam.
  • The march began on 13 April.
  • It reached Vedaranyam on 28 April.
  • Rukmini Lakshmipathi was among the prominent participants.

Other prominent participants included:

  • T. S. S. Rajan
  • Sardar Vedarathnam
  • C. Swaminatha Chettiar
  • K. Santhanam
Arrest and Imprisonment

The Tamil Nadu textbook identifies Rukmini Lakshmipathi as the first woman to undergo punishment for violating the salt laws in the Presidency.

She was imprisoned for her participation.

Her arrest demonstrated that Civil Disobedience had moved beyond symbolic support and included women openly violating colonial law.

Political Representation

Rukmini Lakshmipathi later became:

  • A member of the Madras Legislature
  • Deputy Speaker of the Madras Legislative Assembly
  • Minister for Public Health in the Madras Presidency

She is remembered as:

  • One of the earliest elected women in Madras politics
  • The first woman to serve as a minister in the Madras Presidency
Importance

Her career connected:

  • Women’s suffrage
  • Congress nationalism
  • Civil Disobedience
  • Legislative representation

Do not confuse Rukmini Lakshmipathi with Muthulakshmi Reddy:

  • Rukmini — Salt Satyagraha and Congress politics
  • Muthulakshmi — medicine, legislative reform and resignation in protest during Civil Disobedience
Anjalai Ammal and a Family of Resistance

Anjalai Ammal’s repeated participation and imprisonment show how anti-colonial resistance could become a sustained family commitment.

Early Life and Entry into Politics

Anjalai Ammal belonged to Cuddalore.

She entered nationalist politics during the Non-Cooperation period in 1921.

Her activities extended across several phases:

  • Non-Cooperation
  • Neill Statue agitation
  • Foreign-goods boycott
  • Civil Disobedience
  • Salt Satyagraha period
  • Quit India
Neill Statue Agitation

The statue of Colonel James Neill stood on Mount Road in Madras.

Nationalists opposed it because Neill was associated with brutal repression during the Revolt of 1857.

Anjalai Ammal participated in the agitation demanding the statue’s removal.

Boycott and Picketing

She took part in:

  • Picketing shops selling foreign goods
  • Congress processions
  • Public protests
  • Civil Disobedience activities

In 1930, she was arrested for picketing shops in Madras that sold foreign goods.

Repeated Imprisonment

Anjalai Ammal underwent imprisonment on several occasions.

Accounts of her prison life state that:

  • She was imprisoned while pregnant.
  • She was temporarily released for childbirth.
  • She returned to prison shortly after delivery.

Exact totals given for her imprisonment differ across later accounts. It is safer to state that she underwent repeated and prolonged imprisonment.

Family Participation

Her family also participated in the freedom struggle.

Important associations include:

  • Her husband Murugappan
  • Her daughter Ammakannu
  • Ammakannu was later called Leelavathi
  • Her son-in-law Jamadagni

This shows that nationalist participation could involve an entire household.

Recognition

Anjalai Ammal is often remembered with the title:

  • Jhansi Rani of South India

She later entered the legislature as a Congress representative.

Importance

Anjalai Ammal’s life connected:

  • Grassroots Congress work
  • Women’s street protest
  • Imprisonment
  • Family participation
  • Political representation
Ambujammal and Gandhian Mobilisation

Ambujammal combined Gandhian protest with khadi, women’s organisation, constructive work and service to disadvantaged communities.

Background

S. Ambujammal was born in Madras in 1899.

Her father was:

  • S. Srinivasa Iyengar, a prominent lawyer and nationalist

Ambujammal came from a wealthy family but adopted a simple Gandhian lifestyle.

She was popularly known as:

  • Akkamma
Gandhian Influence

She promoted:

  • Khadi
  • Simplicity
  • Non-violence
  • Village service
  • Women’s education
  • Welfare of the poor

She gave up expensive clothing and jewellery and adopted khadi.

Participation in the Freedom Struggle

Ambujammal participated in:

  • Non-Cooperation
  • Foreign-cloth boycott
  • Civil Disobedience
  • Women’s processions
  • Prabhat pheris
  • Political meetings
  • Volunteer organisation

She was imprisoned during the Civil Disobedience period.

Women’s Mobilisation

She encouraged women to:

  • Join public meetings
  • Wear khadi
  • Boycott imported cloth
  • Participate in processions
  • Support political prisoners
  • Enter social service

She was associated with:

  • Women’s India Association
  • Congress organisation
  • Gandhian women’s networks
Wardha Association

Ambujammal spent time at Gandhi’s Wardha Ashram.

This strengthened her commitment to:

  • Constructive work
  • Village self-sufficiency
  • Women’s training
  • Service to disadvantaged communities
Later Legacy

After Gandhi’s death, she established:

  • Srinivasa Gandhi Nilayam at Teynampet

Its activities included:

  • Educational support
  • Food and medical assistance
  • Training for women

The institution belongs to her later social-service legacy; the chapter should focus primarily on her pre-Independence political participation.

Ammu Swaminathan and Organised Women’s Politics

Ammu Swaminathan connected organised women’s politics, the Congress, Quit India imprisonment and the constitutional transition after colonial rule.

Early Public Role

Ammu Swaminathan was born in 1894 in the Malabar region of the Madras Presidency.

After moving into Madras public life, she became associated with:

  • Women’s rights
  • Congress nationalism
  • Political representation
  • Anti-caste equality
  • Women’s organisations
Women’s India Association

Ammu Swaminathan was an important founding figure in the Women’s India Association at Adyar.

The organisation campaigned for:

  • Women’s franchise
  • Education
  • Legal equality
  • Reform of marriage laws
  • Women’s public participation
Indian National Congress
  • She joined the Indian National Congress in 1934.
  • She participated in nationalist political work.
  • She combined women’s rights with opposition to colonial rule.
Quit India Movement
  • Ammu Swaminathan participated in the Quit India Movement of 1942.
  • She was arrested.
  • She underwent imprisonment during 1943–1944.

Her prison experience is also associated with her rejection of caste prejudice among prisoners.

Constitutional Transition

In 1946, Ammu Swaminathan was elected from Madras to the Constituent Assembly.

Her public career therefore connected:

  • Women’s organisation
  • Congress nationalism
  • Quit India
  • Constitutional democracy
Family Association

Her daughter was:

  • Lakshmi Swaminathan, later Captain Lakshmi Sahgal

Do not merge the two contributions:

  • Ammu Swaminathan — women’s organisation, Congress and Quit India
  • Lakshmi Sahgal — INA and Rani of Jhansi Regiment
Muthulakshmi Reddy and Nationalist Public Life

Muthulakshmi Reddy’s nationalist contribution was expressed mainly through legislative reform and resignation from public office in protest during Civil Disobedience.

Background

Dr. Muthulakshmi Reddy was born in Pudukkottai in 1886.

She became:

  • A medical practitioner
  • Women’s rights campaigner
  • Legislator
  • Social reformer

She was the first woman nominated to the Madras Legislative Council and later became its Deputy President.

Relationship with Nationalism

Muthulakshmi Reddy was influenced by:

  • Annie Besant
  • Sarojini Naidu
  • Mahatma Gandhi

Her main field of work was legislative and social reform rather than continuous street agitation.

Women’s India Association

She was associated with the Women’s India Association and campaigns for:

  • Women’s education
  • Voting rights
  • Health
  • Marriage reform
  • Abolition of harmful practices
Civil Disobedience Protest

In 1930:

  • Gandhi launched the Salt Satyagraha.
  • The government arrested him.
  • Muthulakshmi Reddy resigned from the Madras Legislative Council and its Deputy Presidentship in protest.

Her resignation converted an official constitutional position into an act of political protest.

Legislative Work

Her major reform concerns included:

  • Devadasi dedication
  • Child marriage
  • Women’s education
  • Healthcare
  • Protection of women and children
  • Women’s legal status

Detailed treatment of her social-reform legislation belongs to Chapters 20 and 21.

Essential Distinction

Muthulakshmi Reddy did not play the same role as a marching Salt Satyagrahi.

  • Rukmini Lakshmipathi directly participated in the Vedaranyam campaign.
  • Muthulakshmi Reddy resigned from the legislature in protest against colonial repression.
Women in Civil Disobedience, Boycott and Imprisonment

Women turned boycott, picketing, flag processions and voluntary imprisonment into mass political action, even though many district-level participants remain poorly documented.

Civil Disobedience expanded women’s participation across both urban and rural areas.

Major Activities

Women participated in:

  • Salt-law violation
  • Foreign-cloth boycott
  • Picketing textile shops
  • Liquor-shop picketing
  • Khadi sales
  • Processions
  • Hartals
  • Patriotic singing
  • Flag carrying
  • Fundraising
  • Distribution of pamphlets
Reasons for Women’s Expanded Participation

The Gandhian method enabled women to participate through:

  • Non-violent action
  • Household economic choices
  • Community networks
  • Religious and social gatherings
  • Voluntary arrest
Women and Imprisonment

Women prisoners experienced:

  • Separation from their families
  • Poor sanitation
  • Inadequate medical facilities
  • Hard prison conditions
  • Restrictions on communication
  • Social criticism after release

Imprisonment was politically important because it challenged colonial assumptions that women would remain outside confrontation.

Important Participants

Women connected with Civil Disobedience in Tamil Nadu included:

  • Rukmini Lakshmipathi
  • Anjalai Ammal
  • Ambujammal
  • Vai. Mu. Kothainayaki Ammal
  • Padmasini Ammal
  • Janammal
  • Padmavathi Asher
  • Other district-level Congress volunteers

The surviving records are uneven. Famous leaders were named, while many women appear only in arrest lists and prison registers.

Collective Importance

Women’s participation:

  • Expanded the social base of Congress
  • Strengthened boycott campaigns
  • Normalised women’s presence in public protest
  • Linked political independence with women’s citizenship
  • Produced a generation of women political organisers

The Tamil Nadu textbook describes Civil Disobedience as a mass movement involving women, students, workers and shopkeepers.

Women in Quit India and Underground Mobilisation

During Quit India, women sustained decentralised resistance through communication, shelter, food, funds, pamphlets, strikes and student mobilisation.

Background

The Quit India resolution was adopted on 8 August 1942.

Most recognised Congress leaders were immediately arrested.

The absence of central leadership produced:

  • Local organisation
  • Secret communication
  • Underground pamphlets
  • Decentralised protest
  • Worker and student action
Women’s Forms of Participation

Women contributed by:

  • Carrying messages
  • Hiding documents
  • Sheltering underground activists
  • Distributing pamphlets
  • Organising food and money
  • Joining strikes and processions
  • Maintaining links between local Congress groups
  • Facing arrest

Some of this work was not fully documented because secrecy was essential.

Important Associations
Ammu Swaminathan
  • Participated in Quit India
  • Was arrested
  • Underwent imprisonment
Anjalai Ammal
  • Continued her anti-colonial activity through the Quit India phase
  • Faced repeated colonial repression
Women Students

Women students participated through:

  • Class boycotts
  • Demonstrations
  • Flag processions
  • Distribution of nationalist materials
Wider Tamil Nadu Context

Quit India protests in Tamil Nadu included:

  • Worker strikes
  • Cutting telegraph lines
  • Railway disruption
  • Attacks on symbols of colonial authority
  • Student demonstrations
  • Police firing and arrests

The Tamil Nadu textbook states that all sections of society participated and that many young men and women later joined the INA.

Historical Caution

Women’s underground contribution is often described through family testimony and local histories. Claims about individual sabotage actions should be included only when supported by reliable records.

Journalism, Literature, Music and Cultural Mobilisation

Women journalists, singers and performers used print, music, theatre and cinema to carry nationalist ideas beyond formal political meetings.

Women also challenged colonial rule through print, stage, music and public culture.

This topic should focus only on their nationalist contribution. Their complete literary and artistic careers belong to Chapters 7 and 8.

Vai. Mu. Kothainayaki Ammal

Important associations:

  • Tamil novelist
  • Journalist
  • Editor of Jaganmohini
  • Public speaker
  • Congress activist
  • Khadi supporter

She participated in:

  • Liquor-shop picketing
  • Foreign-cloth boycott
  • Civil Disobedience

She was arrested and imprisoned.

Jaganmohini helped bring:

  • Current affairs
  • Nationalist discussion
  • Women’s writing

to women readers.

K. B. Sundarambal

K. B. Sundarambal used her popularity as a singer and stage artist to support nationalism.

Her contributions included:

  • Singing patriotic songs
  • Promoting Congress campaigns
  • Wearing khadi
  • Campaigning for nationalist candidates
  • Recording songs celebrating sacrifice and freedom

Her powerful public voice helped carry nationalist messages to audiences beyond formal political meetings.

D. K. Pattammal

D. K. Pattammal popularised patriotic compositions, especially songs associated with Subramania Bharati.

Important association:

  • She sang for the film Thyagabhoomi.
  • The film’s nationalist content led to colonial restrictions.
  • Her performances brought patriotic music into homes and public culture.
T. P. Rajalakshmi

T. P. Rajalakshmi was associated with:

  • Tamil theatre
  • Early cinema
  • Patriotic songs
  • Anti-colonial stage performances
  • Women’s social reform

Her songs and plays criticised colonial rule, and some of her work faced censorship.

Importance of Cultural Mobilisation

Music, drama and print:

  • Reached people who did not attend political meetings
  • Evaded restrictions through symbolism
  • Made nationalism emotionally accessible
  • Helped women enter the public sphere
  • Preserved patriotic ideas when the press was censored
Captain Lakshmi Sahgal and the Rani of Jhansi Regiment

Captain Lakshmi Sahgal combined medical service, military command and political representation in the Rani of Jhansi Regiment and Azad Hind government.

Early Life

Captain Lakshmi Sahgal was born:

  • Lakshmi Swaminathan
  • In Madras in 1914

Her parents were:

  • S. Swaminathan, a lawyer
  • Ammu Swaminathan, a political and women’s rights activist

Lakshmi studied:

  • At Queen Mary’s College
  • At Madras Medical College

She qualified as a doctor and later moved to Singapore.

Singapore and the INA

After the British surrender of Singapore in 1942:

  • Lakshmi treated wounded Indian prisoners of war.
  • She came into contact with Indian nationalist networks.
  • Subhas Chandra Bose arrived in Southeast Asia in 1943.
  • Bose proposed the creation of a women’s military regiment.
Rani of Jhansi Regiment

The regiment was named after:

  • Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi

Lakshmi Swaminathan became:

  • Captain Lakshmi
  • Commander of the Rani of Jhansi Regiment

Women volunteers came mainly from Indian communities in:

  • Malaya
  • Singapore
  • Burma

Many were young Tamil women from migrant and plantation families.

Training

The regiment received training in:

  • Military drill
  • Weapons
  • Physical fitness
  • Route marching
  • Camp discipline
  • Nursing
  • First aid

A section of the women received medical and nursing training.

Azad Hind Government

Captain Lakshmi also became:

  • Minister in charge of Women’s Affairs in the Provisional Government of Azad Hind

Her position combined:

  • Military command
  • Women’s mobilisation
  • Political representation
Retreat and Arrest

As the INA and Japanese forces retreated:

  • Members of the regiment assisted the sick and wounded.
  • Lakshmi continued medical work.
  • She was arrested by British forces in Burma in 1945.
  • She returned to India in 1946.
Importance

Captain Lakshmi Sahgal challenged two colonial-era assumptions:

  • That Indians could not organise an independent army
  • That women should remain outside military service

The Rani of Jhansi Regiment became one of the most visible examples of women’s armed anti-colonial mobilisation.

Janaky Thevar and Tamil Diaspora Women in the INA

Janaky Thevar and other Tamil diaspora women demonstrate that INA mobilisation depended heavily on migrant communities in Malaya, Singapore and Burma.

Janaky Thevar

Janaky Athi Nahappan was also known as:

  • Janaky Thevar

She was born in 1925 into a Tamil family in Kuala Lumpur, British Malaya.

Joining the INA

As a teenager:

  • She heard Subhas Chandra Bose’s appeal for support.
  • She donated jewellery to the nationalist cause.
  • She decided to join the Rani of Jhansi Regiment.
  • Her family initially opposed the decision.
  • She persisted and entered military training.
Position in the Regiment

Janaky rose to:

  • The rank of captain
  • A senior command position
  • Second-in-command of the Rani of Jhansi Regiment according to several accounts

She participated in:

  • Military training
  • Recruitment
  • Camp organisation
  • The difficult withdrawal through Burma and Southeast Asia
Tamil Diaspora Participation

The Rani of Jhansi Regiment drew heavily from Indian women living in:

  • Malaya
  • Singapore
  • Burma

Tamil women participated as:

  • Soldiers
  • Nurses
  • Fundraisers
  • Recruiters
  • Cooks
  • Medical assistants
  • Propaganda workers

Many had never lived in India. Their idea of Indian freedom developed through:

  • Migrant community organisations
  • Plantation networks
  • Indian Independence League
  • Bose’s speeches
  • Anti-colonial sentiment
Diaspora Significance

Tamil participation in the INA demonstrates that Tamil Nadu’s freedom-struggle history extended beyond the territorial boundaries of the Madras Presidency.

The diaspora provided:

  • Volunteers
  • Money
  • Jewellery
  • Food
  • Transport
  • Medical assistance
  • Organisational networks
Historical Distinction
  • Lakshmi Sahgal was born and educated in Madras and became the regiment’s commander.
  • Janaky Thevar was born in Malaya to a Tamil family and rose through the regiment’s ranks.
  • Neither should be confused with Rani Lakshmibai, after whom the regiment was named.
Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The final topic consolidates chronology, woman–movement, woman–place, organisation and cultural associations, together with distinctions that prevent common TNPSC errors.

  • 1772 — Muthu Vaduganatha Thevar killed at Kalaiyar Kovil
  • 1780 — Velu Nachiyar recovered Sivaganga
  • 1898 — Birth of Thillaiyadi Valliammai in Johannesburg
  • 1913 — Valliammai joined South African Satyagraha
  • 22 February 1914 — Death of Valliammai
  • 1917 — Women’s India Association established at Adyar
  • 1921 — Anjalai Ammal entered Non-Cooperation activity
  • 1923 — Rukmini Lakshmipathi joined the Congress
  • 1926 — Rukmini attended the international suffrage conference in Paris
  • 1927 — All India Women’s Conference emerged
  • 1927 — Neill Statue agitation
  • 1930 — Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha
  • 1930 — Muthulakshmi Reddy resigned from the Legislative Council
  • 1932 — Major women’s participation and imprisonment during Civil Disobedience

  • 1943 — Rani of Jhansi Regiment organised under Bose
  • 1943–1944 — Ammu Swaminathan imprisoned following Quit India
  • 1945 — Captain Lakshmi arrested in Burma
  • 1946 — Lakshmi returned to India
  • 1946 — Ammu Swaminathan entered the Constituent Assembly

High-Yield Distinctions
Velu Nachiyar versus Kuyili

Velu Nachiyar

  • Queen of Sivaganga
  • Political and military leader
  • Built alliances
  • Recovered the kingdom

Kuyili

  • Commander and associate
  • Connected with a women’s unit
  • Remembered for the ammunition-store attack
Valliammai versus Velu Nachiyar

Valliammai

  • Non-violent Satyagraha
  • South Africa
  • Tamil diaspora
  • Died in 1914

Velu Nachiyar

  • Armed resistance
  • Sivaganga
  • Eighteenth century
  • Restored political authority
Women’s India Association versus All India Women’s Conference

Women’s India Association

  • 1917
  • Adyar
  • Suffrage, legal rights and public participation

All India Women’s Conference

  • 1927
  • Began with women’s education
  • Later expanded into legal and social questions
Rukmini Lakshmipathi versus Muthulakshmi Reddy

Rukmini Lakshmipathi

  • Congress activist
  • Vedaranyam march
  • Imprisoned for salt-law violation
  • Later minister

Muthulakshmi Reddy

  • Doctor and legislator
  • Women’s legal reform
  • Resigned in protest during Civil Disobedience
  • Did not lead the Vedaranyam march
Anjalai Ammal versus Ambujammal

Anjalai Ammal

  • Cuddalore
  • Street protests
  • Repeated imprisonment
  • Family participation

Ambujammal

  • Madras
  • Gandhian constructive work
  • Foreign-cloth boycott
  • Women’s organisation and welfare
Ammu Swaminathan versus Lakshmi Sahgal

Ammu Swaminathan

  • Mother of Lakshmi Sahgal
  • Women’s India Association
  • Congress
  • Quit India
  • Constituent Assembly

Lakshmi Sahgal

  • Daughter of Ammu
  • Doctor
  • INA commander
  • Azad Hind minister
Lakshmi Sahgal versus Janaky Thevar

Lakshmi Sahgal

  • Born in Madras
  • Commander of Rani of Jhansi Regiment
  • Minister for Women’s Affairs

Janaky Thevar

  • Born in Malaya
  • Tamil diaspora volunteer
  • Rose to a senior command position
Gandhian Participation versus INA Participation

Gandhian

  • Non-violent protest
  • Boycott
  • Picketing
  • Khadi
  • Voluntary imprisonment

INA

  • Military training
  • Armed struggle
  • Overseas mobilisation
  • Indian diaspora volunteers
Political Activism versus Social Reform

Political activism

  • Anti-colonial movements
  • Boycott
  • Satyagraha
  • Imprisonment
  • INA

Social reform

  • Education
  • Devadasi abolition
  • Marriage laws
  • Women’s property rights
  • Health

Many women participated in both, but the two roles should not be treated as identical.

Exam Traps
  • Velu Nachiyar was the ruler; Kuyili was her commander and associate.
  • The ammunition-store episode connected with Kuyili is largely preserved through commemorative tradition.
  • Thillaiyadi Valliammai was born and raised in Johannesburg; her family had Tamil roots in Thillaiyadi.
  • The Women’s India Association was established at Adyar in 1917.
  • Rukmini Lakshmipathi participated in the Vedaranyam Salt Satyagraha.
  • Muthulakshmi Reddy resigned from the legislature in protest; she was not the leader of the Vedaranyam march.
  • Anjalai Ammal participated in several phases from Non-Cooperation to Quit India.
  • Ambujammal combined Civil Disobedience with Gandhian constructive work.
  • Ammu Swaminathan was the mother of Captain Lakshmi Sahgal.
  • Lakshmi Sahgal commanded the Rani of Jhansi Regiment.
  • Janaky Thevar belonged to the Tamil diaspora in Malaya.
  • The Rani of Jhansi Regiment was named after Rani Lakshmibai, not Velu Nachiyar.
  • Women’s artistic and literary careers belong to Chapters 7 and 8; only their nationalist contribution belongs here.
  • Detailed women’s social reform and Dravidian movement participation belongs to Chapters 20–29.
